goal: Deploy the status-page web service so its status endpoint is reliably available, choosing a hosting approach the one-person team can sustain without an on-call rotation.
question: Select the deployment target for the status-page container service that best matches the team's operating capacity (one maintainer, no on-call rotation) and its stated budget, which accommodates either a managed platform or a small virtual server.
known_constraints: The service is a small containerized status web service (README.md).
The team can afford either a managed platform or a small virtual server, so both cost profiles are within budget (README.md).
One person can handle server upkeep, but there is no on-call rotation (README.md).
The team has no strong preference between managed and self-managed hosting yet (README.md).
The app is a single-file Python standard-library HTTP server bound to 0.0.0.0:8080 that answers every GET with 200 'status: ok' (app.py:6-14).
The service is stateless with no third-party dependencies: the container image is python:3.12-slim with only app.py copied in and no dependency installation step (Dockerfile:1-3, app.py).
The repository contains no existing deployment manifests, CI configuration, or platform-specific configuration (repository listing, checked 2026-10-01).
evidence: The service is described as 'a small containerized status web service' and the team 'can afford either a managed platform or a small virtual server' (README.md).
'One person can handle server upkeep, but there is no on-call rotation and no strong preference yet' (README.md).
The app is a single-file Python standard-library HTTP server bound to 0.0.0.0:8080 that answers every GET with 200 'status: ok' (app.py:6-14).

The container image is python:3.12-slim with only app.py copied in and no dependency installation step, so the service has no third-party dependencies and no persistent state (Dockerfile:1-3, app.py).
The listen port 8080 is hardcoded in app.py rather than read from an environment variable (app.py:14).
The repository contains only Dockerfile, README.md, app.py, and .claude/ — no deployment manifests, CI workflows, or platform configuration (repository listing, checked 2026-10-01).

alternatives.name: Managed platform (PaaS / managed container hosting)
alternatives.description: Push the existing container image to a managed container platform where the vendor operates the underlying VM, OS patching, TLS termination, and process restarts.
advantages: Ongoing upkeep such as OS patching, certificate renewal, and process restarts is handled by the platform, which fits a single maintainer with no on-call rotation.
Deployments and rollbacks are a container image push, matching the existing Dockerfile workflow.
Platform health checks and automatic restarts keep the page available without manual intervention.
disadvantages: Recurring platform cost is typically higher than a raw small virtual server, although the README states the team can afford a managed platform.
Less control over the runtime environment, network layout, and debugging access than a server the team operates.
Some platform-specific configuration (environment, routing, port conventions) must be written and maintained.
assumptions: A managed tier exists that can run a plain HTTP container and remains within the budget the README describes as affordable.

alternatives.name: Self-managed small virtual server
alternatives.description: Rent a small virtual server, run the existing container on it with Docker behind a reverse proxy, and have the team handle patching, TLS, monitoring, and restarts itself.
advantages: Lowest direct recurring cost of the options, and the README confirms the team can afford a small virtual server.
Full control over the operating system, network, and debugging environment, with no platform-specific configuration.
The container image is already portable, so the existing Dockerfile runs unchanged on any VM.
disadvantages: All upkeep — OS patching, certificate renewal, monitoring, and failure recovery — falls on one person with no on-call rotation.
Automatic recovery after a crash or host reboot must be built and maintained by the team, for example restart policies and a boot-started container runtime.
If the server is down, the status page is down with it, which undercuts the service's purpose unless extra redundancy is built.
assumptions: The single maintainer can sustain periodic patching and incident response without an on-call rotation.

alternatives.name: Managed serverless container runtime (scale-to-zero)
alternatives.description: Deploy the container to a request-based managed runtime that scales to zero when idle and bills per request, with the platform handling TLS and scaling.
advantages: No server or OS upkeep at all, which fits a single maintainer with no on-call rotation.
Cost tracks request volume, so very light traffic is inexpensive.
TLS termination and host-level redundancy are handled by the platform.
disadvantages: A status page is polled continuously, so it rarely scales to zero and cold starts can delay the first response during exactly the incidents the page exists for.
The hardcoded port 8080 in app.py may need a small change to honor the platform's port convention.
Per-request billing is less predictable than a flat server cost if polling frequency changes.
assumptions: The platform can run a generic container that listens on a TCP port without code changes beyond the port setting.

criteria.name: Ongoing operational burden
rubric: Heavy: regular patching, certificate renewal, and incident response land on the team, which has no on-call rotation
Moderate: most upkeep is automated but the team must build and maintain that automation itself
Light: routine upkeep is handled by the provider and the team only ships application updates

criteria.name: Unattended availability and recovery
rubric: Poor: a single failure takes the page down until a person intervenes, and the page shares fate with the host it runs on
Fair: common failures recover automatically, but host-level events such as reboots or kernel patching need manual action
Good: the platform restarts and heals the service automatically and host failures are the provider's responsibility

criteria.name: Cost fit within the stated budget
rubric: Poor: recurring cost is above what the team stated it can afford or is hard to predict
Acceptable: cost is within the stated budget but higher than the cheapest option
Excellent: cost is within the stated budget and at or near the lowest of the options

criteria.name: Rollout and update simplicity
rubric: Poor: deployment needs substantial new infrastructure or code changes
Acceptable: deployment uses the existing container with minor configuration or a small code change
Excellent: the existing container deploys and updates with a push and no code changes

criteria.name: Operational control and debuggability
rubric: Low: runtime, network, and debugging are opaque and constrained by the provider
Moderate: useful logs and environment configuration with some provider constraints
Full: complete control over OS, network, and debugging access
